passage: Gargi, you look tired after the trip to your parents' house, so let me tell you about mine. At twenty-five, every visit home left me sour for days. My father had always compared me with my elder cousin and beaten me down with words whenever my marks slipped. The moment I walked into the flat, I turned twelve again and snapped at everything. One night, on the balcony, I said aloud, "It was unfair, and it still hurts." That was the first time I stopped arguing with the memory. I decided to visit for two days, not five, to leave the old topics alone, and I saw a counsellor. I never announced that my father was forgiven, and I never made him pay. I just stopped acting as if nothing had happened. Harsha

qa.q: How long did Harsha decide each visit should last?
qa.a: Harsha decided on two days instead of five.

qa.q: Why did saying it aloud on the balcony matter to Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha felt relief at admitting the hurt was real, and so stopped arguing with the memory.

qa.q: What steps did Harsha take to manage the visits home?
qa.a: Shorter visits, leaving the old topics alone, and seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had chosen to punish the father forever?
qa.a: The resentment would stay in charge of Harsha's life instead of being acknowledged and managed.

grounding: An elder recalls carrying pain from an unfair childhood that flared on visits home, acknowledging it, choosing limits and seeing a counsellor.

passage:
The train pulled into Lucknow at seven, and by nine Tanvir's shoulders were already up by his ears. Nothing had happened yet. It was just the house. The room where Abbu had praised Yash's marks and torn up Tanvir's report card. The table where Yash always got the bigger piece.

At lunch Abbu said, "Yash has been promoted again." Then, to Tanvir: "And you're still at the same small company?" The old burn rose in Tanvir's throat. He was twenty-six, and he felt twelve.

He went for a walk by the Gomti in the evening. He didn't want to pretend nothing had happened. He also didn't want to spend every visit at war.

So he decided: shorter visits, two days not five. He'd spend more time with Ammi, who had always tried. He'd stop hoping Abbu would change.

That night he looked up a counsellor near his flat in Pune and booked a call for the next week.

qa.q: What did Abbu tear up when Tanvir was a child?
qa.a: He tore up Tanvir's report card.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when Abbu asked about his small company?
qa.a: Tanvir felt an old hurt burn in his throat, feeling like a humiliated twelve-year-old again.

qa.q: What did Tanvir decide about his contact with home?
qa.a: Shorter visits, more time with Ammi, letting go of hoping Abbu would change, and booking a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Tanvir's visits?
qa.a: Ammi likely values time with him and may feel sad that the old favouritism still hurts him.

grounding: The passage shows a young man whose childhood pain flares when he visits home, who acknowledges it, decides what he needs from contact and seeks a counsellor.

passage:
"You're barely eating," Nikita said, finding Jatin on the terrace of their parents' house in Rohtak.

"I can't sit at that table without remembering."

"The belt?"

He nodded. "And the way Papa laughed when I cried. Now he acts like we were a perfect family."

Nikita sat beside him. "I remember too. I just don't say it."

"I keep going back and forth. Some days I want to never come again. Other days I want to scream at him in front of everyone."

"Neither will help you."

"I know." Jatin rubbed his face. "I don't want to pretend. I don't want to punish him forever either. I want... to come for Diwali, stay one night, and leave before it gets bad."

"That sounds fair."

"And my office has a counselling helpline. I think I'll call them."

Nikita squeezed his shoulder. "I'll come with you next Diwali. Same night. We leave together."

qa.a: The parents' house was in Rohtak.

qa.q: How does Jatin feel sitting at his parents' table?
qa.a: Jatin feels hurt and torn, the old pain flaring as he remembers the belt and his father's laughter.

qa.q: What does Jatin decide about contact with his father?
qa.a: To visit briefly, one night at Diwali, not pretending but not punishing forever, and to call his office's counselling helpline.

qa.q: How does Nikita experience the family's past?
qa.a: Nikita remembers the pain too but keeps quiet, and she chooses to stand by Jatin.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young man whose childhood pain flares at home, who acknowledges the hurt, decides what contact he needs and plans to see a counsellor.
